items.explanation: Taylor's 'scientific management' broke jobs into timed motions to squeeze maximum output from workers — the intellectual seed of the assembly line.
options: B. Guaranteed higher wages and better conditions
C. Sought maximum efficiency in factory operations
items.stem: Frederick W. Taylor's methods, embraced by many factory owners,

option_explanations.A: Taylor's system was about squeezing output from workers, not about helping immigrants assimilate. 'Scientific management' treated workers as machines to be timed and optimized, not as newcomers to be welcomed.
option_explanations.B: The opposite of how Taylorism worked in practice. Taylor's methods were meant to raise output — often by cutting wages per unit and speeding up work — not to guarantee workers higher pay or better conditions.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Frederick W. Taylor's 'scientific management' broke factory jobs into timed, standardized motions to wring maximum efficiency and output from every worker — the intellectual seed of the assembly line.
option_explanations.D: Taylor's system deskilled work on purpose: by breaking jobs into tiny, timed motions, it required less skill and less training from workers, not more.

items.explanation: Industrial cities did cluster workers near factories around a downtown of offices and banks, with saloons in working-class wards — but by 1890 steam, not water, powered most industry.
options: A. Workers lived near factories close to downtown
B. Factories were sited near water for power
C. Downtowns held offices, banks, and insurers
items.stem: All of the following describe the late-nineteenth-century industrial city EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: True of the era: industrial workers really did live near factories close to downtown, since they walked to work. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception. By 1890 steam engines, not waterpower, drove most industry, so factories no longer had to sit beside rivers for power. Water-powered mill towns belonged to an earlier industrial era.
option_explanations.C: True of the era: downtowns really did hold offices, banks, and insurers while workers lived in wards around them. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: True of the era: saloons really did dot working-class neighborhoods, serving as social centers for immigrant workers. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Tarbell's History ran in McClure's (1902-1904) and became ammunition for the Progressive assault on the trusts. In 1911 the Supreme Court, applying the Sherman Antitrust Act, dissolved Standard Oil into 34 separate companies -- the direct legislative and judicial answer to the concentration she documented.
options: A. The repeal of all federal business regulation
B. Rockefeller's election to the presidency
C. Progressive Era antitrust action culminating in the 1911 breakup of Standard Oil
D. The nationalization of the American oil industry
items.stem: The concentration of power Tarbell describes helped produce which of the following?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year... a sum which, if distributed among the thousands of stockholders, would make every one of them rich — and yet the company was built up by methods which have made it the most hated corporation in the country."
—Ida Tarbell, on Standard Oil, 1904 (abridged and paraphrased)

option_explanations.A: The opposite of what happened. Tarbell's expose fueled demands for more federal business regulation, not less — her work helped bring on the Progressive Era's antitrust and regulatory push.
option_explanations.B: Rockefeller never ran for president. The political result of Tarbell's work was not his election but the legal attack on his company.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Tarbell's History of the Standard Oil Company (1902–1904) became ammunition for the Progressive assault on the trusts; in 1911 the Supreme Court, applying the Sherman Antitrust Act, dissolved Standard Oil into 34 separate companies.
option_explanations.D: The American oil industry was never nationalized. The government's answer was breaking Standard Oil up through antitrust law, not taking it over.
